'''''Zanthoxylum armatum''''', also called '''winged prickly ash''' or '''rattan pepper''' in English, is a [[species]] of [[plant]] in the family [[Rutaceae]]. It is an aromatic, deciduous, spiny [[shrub]] growing to {{convert|3.5|m|ft}} in height, endemic from [[Pakistan]] across to [[Southeast Asia]] and up to [[Korea]] and [[Japan]]. It is one of the sources of the spice [[Sichuan pepper]], and also used in folk medicine, essential oil production and as an ornamental garden plant.

==Description==
The plant grows as a woody climber, a shrub or a tree, up to {{convert|3.5|m|ft}} in height.<ref name="foc">{{cite web |title=31. ''Zanthoxylum armatum'' Candolle, Prodr. 1: 727. 1824. |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=242355514 |website=Flora of China |publisher=eFloras.org |access-date=2 January 2021}}</ref><ref name="hertog"/> It is deciduous, with subsessile, opposite leaves of lanceolate, obovate or elliptic shape. Branchlets and leaves have prickles/spines. The young branchlets and inflorescence rachises are glabrous or the young branches are sparsely pubescent. The rachis of the leaves is pubescent glabrous or rust-colored and has wings to 6 mm on each side, hence it common English name, this is one of the anatomical features distinguishing it from other ''Zanthoxylum'' species.<ref>{{cite web |title=1. ''Zanthoxylum Linnaeus'', Sp. Pl. 1: 270. 1753. |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=135262 |website=Flora of China |publisher=eFloras.org |access-date=2 January 2021}}</ref> Other anatomically separating features are generally faint secondary veins of leaflet blades, especially adaxially, with 7-15 on each side of midvein; the anthers of the male flowers are yellow before anthesis; and the gynoecium of the female flowers is 1-3-carpelled. Fruit follicles are purplish-red, about 4-5mm in diameter, while the seeds are black and 3-4mm in size. The shrub flowers in [[China]] from April to May, and fruits from August to October, in Nepal it flowers during the same months, while the fruit is available all year round. In India, flowering is from March to April.<ref name="flowers"/>

==Taxonomy==
The species was described by the eminent Swiss botanist [[Augustin Pyramus de Candolle]] in 1824.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Zanthoxylum armatum'' DC., Prodr. [A. P. de Candolle] 1: 727, sphalm. (1824). |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/775583-1 |website=International Plant Name Index (IPNI) |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |access-date=2 January 2021}}</ref>

The plant has an accepted infraspecific, ''Zanthoxylum armatum'' var. ''ferrugineum'' ([[Alfred Rehder|Rehder]] & [[Ernest Henry Wilson|E.H.Wilson]]) [[Cheng Chiu Huang|C.C.Huang]].<ref name=powo/> This variety has rust-coloured pubescent young branchlets and inflorescence rachises distinguishing it from the nominative variety.<ref name="foc"/><ref name="focvf">{{cite web |title=31b. ''Zanthoxylum armatum'' var. ''ferrugineum'' (Rehder & E. H. Wilson) C. C. Huang, Guihaia. 7: 1. 1987. |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=242355516 |website=Flora of China |publisher=eFloras.org |access-date=2 January 2021}}</ref>

==Distribution==
''Zanthoxylum armatum'' is native to parts of East and Southeast Asia, and the north of the Indian sub-continent. It is naturalised in several regions.<ref name=powo>{{Cite POWO | id = 775583-1 |title=''Zanthoxylum armatum'' DC. | access-date = 11 November 2024}}</ref><ref name="foc"/> Regions where it occurs are: [[Japan]]; [[Ryukyu Islands|Nansei-shoto/Ryukyu Islands]]; [[Korea]]; North-Central, South-Central & Southeast China, specifically [[Anhui]], [[Fujian]], South [[Gansu]], [[Guangdong]], [[Guangxi]], [[Guizhou]], South [[Henan]], [[Hubei]], [[Hunan]], [[Jiangsu]], [[Jiangxi]], [[Shaanxi]], [[Shandong]], South [[Shanxi]], [[Sichuan]],  [[Xizang]], [[Yunnan]], and [[Zhejiang]]; northern [[Taiwan]]; [[Philippines]]; [[Vietnam]]; [[Laos]]; [[Thailand]]; [[Myanmar]]; [[Bangladesh]]; [[India]], including [[Assam]]; [[Bhutan]]; [[Nepal]]; [[Tibet]]; the Eastern and Western Himalayas; Kashmir; and [[Pakistan]], and possibly [[Indonesia]].<ref name="foc"/> It has been naturalised in Northeast [[Argentina]] and the North [[Caucasus]].

The variety ''ferrugineum'' occurs in North-Central, South-Central & Southeast China, specifically in Guangdong, Guangxi, Guizhou, Hunan, Shaanxi, Sichuan and Yunnan.<ref name=powoferr/><ref name="focvf"/>

==Habitat & Ecology==
''Z. armatum'' grows in many habitats below 3100m.<ref name="foc"/> In the [[Salyan District, Nepal]], the shrub grows in the understorey of lower altitude ''[[Pinus roxburghii]]'' forests, alongside ''[[Aesculus indica]]'' and ''[[Bassia latifolia]]'', and in higher altitude oak forests (''[[Quercus incana]]'' & ''[[Quercus lanuginosa|Q. lanuginosa]]''), where they associate with ''[[Rhododendron arboreum]]'' & ''[[Lyonia ovalifolia]]''.<ref name="hertog">{{cite journal |last1=den Hertog |first1=W.H. |last2=Wiersum |first2=K.F. |title=Timur (''Zanthoxylum armatum'') Production in Nepal: Dynamics in Nontimber Forest Resource Management |journal=Mountain Research and Development |date=2000 |volume=20 |issue=2 May |pages=136–145 |doi=10.1659/0276-4741(2000)020[0136:TZAPIN]2.0.CO;2 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Birds like the fruits and widely disseminate the plants.

==Vernacular names==
''Z. armatum'' is known by a number of vernacular names. In China, the plant and its fresh berries are known as ''téngjiāo'' ({{zh||c=藤椒}}), while the dried seeds are known as ''qinghuajiao'' ({{zh||c=青花椒}}) or ''majiao'' ({{zh||c=麻椒}}). ==Uses==
[[File:Sechuan pepper.jpg|thumb|A handful of dried green Sichuan pepper]]

The fruit and seeds of the plant are used as a spice, ''[[timut pepper]]'', related to ''[[Sichuan pepper]]'',<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Xiang|first1=Li|last2=Liu|first2=Yue|date=April 2016|title=The Chemical and Genetic Characteristics of Szechuan Pepper (''Zanthoxylum bungeanum'' and ''Z. armatum'') Cultivars and Their Suitable Habitat|journal=Frontiers in Plant Science|volume=7|page=467|doi=10.3389/fpls.2016.00467|pmid=27148298 |pmc=4835500 |doi-access=free}}</ref> but less pungent, while the bark, fruit and seeds are used in indigenous medicines in India, Nepal and Thailand.<ref name="flowers"/><ref name="grin"/><ref name="hertog"/> The plant is also a source of an essential oil, ''Wartara Oil'', and the shrub is also grown as an ornamental garden plant.

Timur is prominent in Nepalese cuisine, where it is prized for its aroma and numbing sensation, often used in cooking sauces, pickles, meats, dumplings, and various other dishes. It is especially characteristic of the food of Western Nepal.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The taste of timmur: A unique Nepali spice |url=https://annapurna-express.prixa.net/story/45659/ |access-date=2026-09-05 |website=The Annapurna Express |language=Nepali}}</ref>

In the Salyan district of Nepal, the parts used in medicine are harvested primarily of export to India. The plants grow in state-controlled, community-controlled and private lands, resulting in a variety of access regimes, harvesting regimes and management practices, leading to a conclusion that in general the effects of supply and demand on [[Non-timber forest products]] (NTFP) cannot be generalised, but are specific to each product and place.<ref name="hertog"/>

Extracts have been shown to inhibit the growth of  [[Porphyromonas gingivalis]] – the main bacteria involved in [[Periodontal disease]] and suspected cause of [[Alzheimer's disease]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Carrol |first=Danielle H. |last2=Chassagne |first2=François |last3=Dettweiler |first3=Micah |last4=Quave |first4=Cassandra L. |date=2020-10-08 |title=Antibacterial activity of plant species used for oral health against Porphyromonas gingivalis |journal=PLOS ONE |volume=15 |issue=10 |article-number=e0239316 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0239316 |issn=1932-6203|doi-access=free |pmc=7544490 }}</ref>
